section.title: Paul's Joy at Their Repentance
section.sectionRationale: Resuming the appeal broken off at 6:13, Paul reopens his heart and then pours out the relief and joy that Titus's report has brought him. His severe letter had grieved the Corinthians, but their grief proved to be godly sorrow that produced genuine repentance. Here Paul gives the classic distinction between godly sorrow that leads to salvation without regret and worldly sorrow that only brings death, and rejoices that his confidence in them has been fully restored.
section.thesis: Godly sorrow, unlike the worldly grief that ends in death, produces repentance that leads to salvation without regret; and the fruit of such repentance in the Corinthians has turned Paul's anguish into overflowing comfort, joy, and restored confidence.
section.frameNote: Three movements: the reopened heart and Paul's comfort at Titus's arrival; the heart of the passage, godly sorrow versus worldly sorrow and the fruit of true repentance; and Paul's restored confidence and shared joy at Titus's refreshment.

units.label: Comforted by Titus's arrival
units.note: make room for us in your hearts

verses.text: Make room for us in your hearts. We have wronged no one, we have corrupted no one, we have exploited no one.
I do not say this to condemn you. I have said before that you so occupy our hearts that we live and die together with you.
Great is my confidence in you; great is my pride in you; I am filled with encouragement; in all our troubles my joy overflows.
For when we arrived in Macedonia, our bodies had no rest, but we were pressed from every direction; conflicts on the outside, fears within.
But God, who comforts the downcast, comforted us by the arrival of Titus,
and not only by his arrival, but also by the comfort he had received from you. He told us about your longing, your mourning, and your zeal for me, so that I rejoiced all the more.

units.label: Godly sorrow and worldly sorrow
units.note: repentance that leads to salvation without regret

verses.text: Even if I caused you sorrow by my letter, I do not regret it. Although I did regret it, for I see that my letter caused you sorrow, but only for a short time,

yet now I rejoice, not because you were made sorrowful, but because your sorrow led you to {{metanoia|repentance}}. For you felt the sorrow that God had intended, and so were not harmed in any way by us.
Godly {{lype|sorrow}} brings repentance that leads to salvation without regret, but worldly sorrow brings death.

Consider what this godly sorrow has produced in you: what earnestness, what eagerness to clear yourselves, what indignation, what alarm, what longing, what zeal, what vindication! In every way you have proved yourselves to be innocent in this matter.
So even though I wrote to you, it was not on account of the one who did wrong or the one who was harmed, but rather that your earnestness on our behalf would be made clear to you in the sight of God.
On account of this, we are encouraged. In addition to our own encouragement, we were even more delighted by the joy of Titus. For his spirit has been refreshed by all of you.
Indeed, I was not embarrassed by anything I had boasted to him about you. But just as everything we said to you was true, so our boasting to Titus has proved to be true as well.
And his affection for you is even greater when he remembers that you were all obedient as you welcomed him with fear and trembling.
I rejoice that I can have complete confidence in you.

metanoia.gloss: Repentance, literally a change of mind that turns into a change of life. It is more than regret or feeling bad; it is a turning of the whole person away from sin and back to God. Paul rejoices not that the Corinthians were saddened but that their sorrow produced this genuine turning. True metanoia leads to salvation and leaves no regret, because it is the fruit God intended.

lype.gloss: Sorrow, grief, pain of heart. Paul distinguishes two kinds. Godly sorrow is grief felt as God intends, over sin against Him, and it drives one to repentance and life. Worldly sorrow is mere remorse over consequences, wounded pride, or being caught, and it festers into death. The same word covers both; what matters is the direction the sorrow takes the heart.

basic.context: Paul picks up the appeal he left at 6:13, asking the Corinthians to make room for him in their hearts. He had come into Macedonia worn down and anxious, but God comforted him through Titus, who brought good news: Paul's painful letter had grieved the Corinthians, and their grief had turned into real repentance. Paul then explains the difference between godly sorrow, which leads to life, and worldly sorrow, which leads to death, and rejoices that his confidence in them is now complete.
basic.hermeneutics: This is a deeply pastoral passage about how loving correction is meant to work. Paul is relieved not that they were hurt but that their hurt bore the right fruit. The key is verses 10 and 11: read the difference between the two sorrows, and notice the concrete evidences of true repentance Paul lists. Sorrow is not the goal; repentance that turns to God and issues in changed action is.
basic.originalLanguages: The turning point is metanoia, repentance, a change of mind that becomes a change of life, not mere regret. Paul contrasts two kinds of lype, sorrow: godly grief over sin that drives one to God and life, and worldly grief that festers into death. The same pain can run in opposite directions.
basic.typology: The prophets called Israel to return to the Lord with true repentance rather than empty remorse, and Paul's godly sorrow fulfills that call under the new covenant. The comfort God brings to the downcast through Titus reflects the God who comforts His afflicted people throughout Scripture, ultimately in Christ.
basic.christ: The salvation to which godly sorrow leads is salvation in Christ, whose death makes repentance a road to life rather than despair. Because Christ has borne sin, the sorrow of the penitent is not crushing but hopeful, leading to reconciliation. Paul's ministry of correction serves Christ's work of presenting a pure and restored church to Himself.
basic.god: God is the one who comforts the downcast and who intends a sorrow that heals. He stands behind the whole process: the letter, the grief, the repentance, and the joy are all under His sight and for His purpose. He is the God who turns even painful discipline toward the salvation and good of His people.
basic.crossReferences: Psalm 51 is the model prayer of godly sorrow and repentance. Matthew 27 shows the worldly remorse of Judas that ended in death. Hebrews 12 speaks of the painful discipline that yields the peaceful fruit of righteousness.
basic.oneStory: God has always called His people not merely to feel bad over sin but to turn back to Him and live. Here that turning bears fruit through Paul's hard letter, and joy replaces grief. It is the pattern of the whole gospel: sorrow over sin, met by the God who comforts, leading through repentance to salvation in Christ.

context.literary:
The section is a frame within a frame. On the outside, 7:2 to 4 and 7:13 to 16 mark the beginning and the end with the same words: confidence, pride, joy, encouragement, and the heart. In the middle, 7:5 to 7 tells the story of Titus, and 7:8 to 12 holds the teaching about sorrow. So the section has the form of a ring: heart, comfort, sorrow and repentance, comfort, heart. The doctrinal centre of the ring is verse 10, and the ring explains why it is there: the doctrine of true repentance is not abstract, it is the story of what has happened to people Paul loves.

The section is also the second half of a frame that began earlier. In 2:12 to 13 Paul left Troas with no peace because he had not found Titus, and then the narrative broke off to speak of the triumph of the gospel and of the ministry of the new covenant. Now, at 7:5, the narrative resumes with the same word of arrival in Macedonia and the same absence of rest. Five chapters of theology sit inside the gap, which is a deliberate way to tell the story: the theology is the explanation of how Paul was able to carry on.

The central verse is built on three antitheses of its own, and the list of verse 11 is a series of seven nouns, earnestness, eagerness to clear themselves, indignation, alarm, longing, zeal and vindication, set out as an escalating run. The effect is that Paul replaces a definition of repentance with a portrait of it. The close, verse 16, turns on the word confidence and answers the opening of verse 4, so that Paul ends where he began, but now with the matter settled.
context.historical:
To read the passage well it helps to reconstruct the sequence. Paul had made a painful visit to Corinth, 2:1. He had afterward written a severe letter out of great distress, 2:4, and sent Titus with it, probably also to organize the collection, 8:6. He then left Ephesus and travelled to Troas, found no Titus, and went on to Macedonia, 2:12 to 13. There, with fighting without and fear within, he waited for news. Titus came, and with him the report that the church had responded.

Corinth was a city in which public shame and honour mattered intensely, and a rebuke in a letter that would be read aloud before the whole congregation carried real social risk. The church could have answered with defensiveness or with a split, and Paul feared one of those. What Titus reported was neither. The response had the marks of a community that had taken a correction to heart. The wronged and the wrongdoer of 7:12 refer to the case of discipline dealt with in 2:5 to 11, and the likelier reading is that the church had dealt with the offender, which is why Paul now urges forgiveness there.

Paul also reveals how much was at stake for him personally. He admits that he regretted sending the letter for a time, 7:8. This honesty is rare in ancient letters, where a writer seldom confessed doubts about his own course. The passage is therefore an unusually open window into the mind of an apostle and into how first century churches managed conflict.
context.canonical:
The distinction between two kinds of sorrow has deep roots in Scripture. The prophets pictured repentance as a return, with a heart torn rather than garments, Joel 2:12 to 13, and Hosea 6:1 gives the invitation, Come, let us return to the LORD. Psalm 51:17 names the offering God wants: a broken spirit, a broken and contrite heart. Isaiah 57:15 and 66:2 say that God dwells with the contrite and esteems the one who trembles at His word. These are the texts that lie behind Paul's godly sorrow.

The other half of the contrast has biblical portraits too. Esau wept and sought a blessing with tears, yet Hebrews 12:16 to 17 says he found no place for repentance. Judas was filled with remorse and returned the money, Matthew 27:3 to 5, and then died by his own hand. Peter, by contrast, wept bitterly after his denial, Luke 22:62, and was restored, John 21. The difference between these two weeping men is the meaning of verse 10.

The New Testament repeatedly calls for deeds that fit repentance, as John the Baptist does in Luke 3:8 and Paul in Acts 26:20. Hebrews 12:11 treats painful discipline as a fruit of the Father's love. The church's long practice of pastoral correction and restoration, from 1 Corinthians 5 to Galatians 6:1, belongs to the same stream.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
Paul writes this paragraph to complete a reconciliation. The Corinthians had been hurt by his letter, and he wants them to understand two things at once: that he did not enjoy hurting them, and that the hurt did them good. He is walking a narrow path. He must not make the sorrow sound trivial, since he admits it was real, and he must not let them wallow in it, since sorrow in itself is not the goal. The goal is repentance, and the evidence of repentance is a changed heart toward God and toward him.

He also means to hold up for them a picture of themselves that they can recognise and be glad of. The list in verse 11 is a mirror, and it is a kind one. In every way you have proved yourselves to be innocent in this matter is a pastoral judgment that lifts the cloud, and it is intended to prepare the ground for the appeal about the collection that follows in chapters 8 and 9. People whose confidence has been restored are more ready to be generous.

Finally, Paul tells them why he wrote at all: not on account of the one who did wrong or the one who was harmed, but that their earnestness on our behalf would be made clear to them in the sight of God, 7:12. His aim was their spiritual health and the truth of their bond with the apostles, not a verdict on an individual.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
The travel story and the report from Titus are descriptions of a particular history, and the passage does not command anyone to send harsh letters or to expect a rapid response. It would be a serious misuse to take Paul's relief as a licence for speaking sharply and assuming that any resulting pain is godly.

The teaching in verses 10 and 11 is prescriptive in the sense that it names what true repentance looks like, and so gives a way to test oneself and to help others. It is not a checklist of seven emotions that must be felt in order. The list shows a whole turning: concern, a desire to put things right, a hatred of wrong, a healthy fear, a longing for restoration, a jealous love of what is right, and a readiness to see justice done.

A further caution is needed about how to apply it to others. Paul speaks of what he saw in a community he knew well and could see the effects of. Believers are not given the right to judge the inner sorrow of another person, and the right place for discernment is among those who are in a relationship of care and responsibility. For oneself, the verses are a searching question: when I am convicted, does the sorrow push me toward God, or toward hiding and self punishment?

debates.question: What was the severe or tearful letter Paul refers to?

views.label: A lost letter written between 1 and 2 Corinthians
views.case: Many hold that Paul wrote a now lost, painful letter after the sorrowful visit, distinct from 1 Corinthians, since the emotional distress described does not match 1 Corinthians well.

views.label: First Corinthians itself
views.case: Others identify the severe letter with 1 Corinthians, which contains sharp rebuke, taking Paul's language of causing sorrow to refer to that canonical letter.

debates.bearing: The doctrine of the passage stands either way; whichever letter is meant, the point is that loving, painful correction produced godly sorrow and true repentance rather than harm.

debates.question: What is the difference between godly sorrow and worldly sorrow?

views.label: A difference of object and direction
views.case: Godly sorrow grieves over sin against God and turns the heart to Him in repentance and life; worldly sorrow grieves over consequences, shame, or being caught and turns inward to despair and death.

views.label: A difference chiefly of outcome
views.case: Some stress the fruit as the test: the same feeling of grief is godly if it ends in repentance and salvation, worldly if it ends in death, so the outcome reveals which it was.

debates.bearing: The two readings reinforce each other: sorrow rightly directed toward God bears the fruit of repentance and life, and the presence of that fruit, listed in verse 11, is how godly sorrow is known.

study.originalLanguages:
Beyond metanoia and lype, five features of the Greek carry weight.

The first is metamelomai, to regret, which Paul uses of himself in 7:8, I regretted it, and which he sets against the word in verse 10, ametameleton, without regret. These words are not synonyms of metanoia. Metamelomai describes a feeling of regret, which can be shallow or can be bitter; metanoia describes a change of mind and direction. That is why Matthew 27:3 says Judas, seized with remorse, uses metamelētheis, a word of regret, and does not say he repented. Paul's wording therefore says that repentance leads to a salvation that no one will ever have cause to regret. The same word appears in a related form in Romans 11:29, where God's gifts and call are irrevocable, literally not subject to regret.

The second is the phrase kata theon, according to God, repeated in verses 9, 10 and 11. It describes a sorrow measured by God's standard and held in His sight, and the repetition shows the key. Godly sorrow is not defined by its depth of feeling but by its relation to God.

The third is the catalogue of verse 11, which names seven results: spoude, earnestness, apologia, a defence or clearing of themselves, aganaktesis, indignation, phobos, alarm or fear, epipothesis, longing, zelos, zeal, and ekdikesis, which the BSB renders vindication and which carries the sense of seeing justice done. The seven nouns are linked in the Greek by a repeated word meaning yes indeed or but rather, which gives the list a breathless rush. Each is a way in which they turned: toward the truth, toward Paul, toward the wronged and toward justice.

The fourth is hagnos, the word the BSB gives as innocent in verse 11. It means pure, clean, and it appears in 11:2 of a pure virgin presented to Christ. Paul is not saying they were guiltless in the matter; he says they have shown themselves clean now in how they dealt with it.

The fifth is the repeated parakaleo family in verses 6, 7 and 13, comfort or encouragement. The same family opened the letter in 1:3 to 7, where God is the Father of all comfort. The word for the downcast in 7:6, tapeinoi, is the humble or low, and God's comfort of them is the continuing pattern of the God who lifts the lowly. In verse 15, phobou kai tromou, fear and trembling, is a phrase Paul uses elsewhere, as in 1 Corinthians 2:3 and Philippians 2:12, for a reverent seriousness before God.

typology.fulfillment: When Nathan said, You are the man, David answered, I have sinned against the LORD, 2 Samuel 12:13, and Psalm 51 gives his prayer. The sorrow is of the kind Paul calls godly: it takes God's side against itself, it pleads for cleansing and it expects restoration. The correspondence is that grief takes a person toward God and then toward obedience. The escalation is that David's repentance depended on a promise of mercy given to a king, while Paul's depends on a finished work, the cross. The type falls short in that David's sin had lasting consequences, and in that repentance by itself could not remove sin; the cleansing came ultimately by the blood of the covenant.

typology.type: The return of the prodigal, Luke 15:17 to 24
typology.fulfillment: The son in the far country came to himself, resolved to go home and said to his father, I have sinned against heaven and against you. The pattern is the movement Paul describes: a change of mind that leads to a change of direction and an act. The father's running to meet him is the picture of the God who comforts the downcast. The escalation is that the parable is Jesus' own picture of what His coming makes possible, so that repentance meets a welcome and not only a hearing. The type falls short in that it shows the welcome but not yet the cost, which is revealed at the cross.

Two disciples failed Jesus in the same night, and both were seized by grief. Judas returned the money and ended in despair. Peter wept bitterly and, after the resurrection, was restored with a question and a commission. They are the plainest narrative illustration of verse 10, the same pain going two ways. The correspondence is that grief alone does not decide the outcome; what matters is where it turns. The escalation is that the difference between them is not their sin but their turning to the Lord. The type falls short in that two men do not exhaust the possibilities, and it would be a mistake to treat every tearful person as a Judas or every restored one as a Peter.

typology.type: The prophetic call to a torn heart, Joel 2:12 to 13
typology.fulfillment: Joel said that the LORD wanted the people to return with weeping and mourning, and to tear their hearts and not their garments. The prophet made repentance a matter of the inner person and promised that God is gracious and compassionate. Paul's godly sorrow lives in that tradition. The escalation is that the promise of a gracious God has been made complete in the gospel, and that the Spirit given in the new covenant produces the heart Joel asked for. The type falls short in that the prophet's call was addressed to a nation facing a disaster, whereas Paul writes to a church already reconciled and being brought to maturity.

study.christ:
Christ is not named in verses 2 to 16, yet He stands behind all of them, and the way He does so is worth tracing carefully. The phrase salvation without regret in verse 10 points to a salvation that has a ground, and that ground is the cross. Repentance cannot create a salvation; it is the way a person turns toward the one who provides it. Without Christ, godly sorrow would be only sorrow, with nothing to meet it. With Christ, the broken and contrite heart is met by the one who bore sin on the tree, 1 Peter 2:24.

The passage also presents Christ's own way of dealing with sinners as the model for Paul's. The apostle wounds in order to heal, and the church that took the correction well is shown to be like the sheep that hear the Shepherd's voice, John 10:27. Jesus Himself corrected severely, as in the letters to the churches in Revelation 3:19, Those whom I love I rebuke and discipline, so be earnest and repent, and Paul's word zeal in 7:11 belongs to the same word family as the be earnest of that verse.

The difference between the two sorrows is finally the difference between Peter and Judas. Both met the same Lord on the night of His arrest. One looked at the Lord and wept and was restored, Luke 22:61 to 62. The other looked only at himself. In Christ's resurrection appearances, He restores Peter with a threefold question, John 21:15 to 17, and shows that no fall is too deep for restoration. The cross is thus the reason repentance is not a ladder we have to climb but a door that has been opened.

We must not make Christ the hidden subject of every detail, as if Titus were a type of the Saviour. The consistent teaching is that repentance, forgiveness and the restored joy of the church all rest on the finished work of Christ. Paul's confidence in the Corinthians is, in the end, confidence in the work that Christ has begun in them, Philippians 1:6.
study.god:
The first thing the passage shows about God is His particular attention to the downcast. Paul had been pressed from every direction, with fears within, and the verdict of the text is that God, who comforts the downcast, comforted him. It does not say that God took the pressure away at once, or that He sent an angel. It says that He comforted by the arrival of a friend. God's comfort has a human face. He works through the coming of Titus and through the news Titus carried, so that comfort passes from the Corinthians to Titus to Paul and then on to the reader.

The second is that God intends sorrow to do good. The phrase the sorrow that God had intended, in verse 9, is a short statement of providence. He is not the author of the Corinthians' sin, but He is able to use a painful letter, a painful visit and a painful discipline for their healing. This is a God who is not afraid of tears and who does not waste them. The answer to the question why would a good God allow such sadness is, in part, that the pain was aimed at life, not death. That matches Hebrews 12:10 and 11, which say that He disciplines us for our good, so that we may share His holiness.

The third is the way God holds together mercy and truth. The passage does not soften the offence, yet it brings forgiveness and restored fellowship. A God who only comforted would not correct; a God who only corrected would not comfort. Here the two belong to a single act of love. The distinction in verse 10 depends on this: because God is both holy and merciful, sorrow can turn toward Him with hope.

Finally, God is the one who sees the heart. The earnestness of the Corinthians is made clear, Paul says, in the sight of God. Worship is therefore not display but honesty before the one to whom all hearts are open. The proper response is gratitude for His comfort and a readiness to receive His correction with the same trust.

crossReferences.note: David's prayer after Nathan's rebuke is the great example of godly sorrow. It appeals to God's unfailing love, owns the sin as against God, asks for cleansing and ends with the offering of a broken and contrite heart. Reading it beside Paul's list shows that earnestness, defence and longing all appear in David's own prayer.

Judas was filled with remorse and returned the silver, yet he went away and hanged himself. The word the Gospel uses is the word of regret, not of turning. He admitted the wrong and even made a gesture of restitution, which shows that regret and confession alone do not amount to repentance if the heart turns away from God.

The Lord turned and looked at Peter, and Peter went out and wept bitterly. The same night, the same sin of failing Christ, and a very different end. It is the clearest narrative picture of sorrow that is turned toward the Lord and therefore leads to restoration.

The Father disciplines those He loves, and the discipline, painful at the time, yields a harvest of righteousness and peace for those trained by it. It supplies the doctrine behind 7:9: the sorrow God intends is the sorrow of a Father's training and not the anger of a judge.

God is the Father of mercies and the God of all comfort, who comforts us so that we may comfort others. 7:6 to 7 is the story of that comfort travelling: God comforts Paul by Titus, and Titus was himself comforted by the Corinthians. It shows that the opening of the letter was not a pious flourish but a lived account.

Paul explains why he wrote with tears, not to cause pain but to show his abounding love, and then urges the church to forgive and comfort the offender. It is the earlier half of the same story and shows what the church's discipline had been aimed at and how Paul hoped it would end.

The LORD calls the people to return with all the heart and to tear their hearts, not their garments, since He is gracious and compassionate. Paul's godly sorrow belongs to this call, and the verse helps explain why outward display of grief in itself is not the measure.

Esau sought the blessing with tears and found no place for repentance. The passage is the nearest Old Testament figure for worldly sorrow, which weeps over loss and consequence without turning back to God.

John the Baptist tells the crowds to produce fruit in keeping with repentance. It matches the list of verse 11, in which true sorrow is shown not by feeling alone but by earnestness, a readiness to clear oneself and a zeal to put things right.

The son in the far country came to himself and set out for home. The text gives the plain shape of the change of mind and direction that Paul calls repentance, and the father's greeting shows what the repentant meet.

study.oneStory:
The Bible is the story of a good creation, a rebellion, a rescue and a restoration, and repentance is the hinge on which individual lives and whole communities turn from the second to the fourth. Adam hid; the woman and the man shifted blame; Cain went away from the presence of the LORD. From the first chapters, the human response to guilt has been to flee. The long story of grace is about a God who goes after the fugitive and turns him around.

Looking back, this passage answers the question that haunts Israel's history. The people rebelled, were disciplined and were exiled, and the prophets kept calling for a return of the heart. Some returned and some only mourned. Paul shows what the true response looks like when it happens: grief that takes God's side, a readiness to put wrongs right, and a restored fellowship. It also answers the troubled question of the earlier chapters of this letter, whether painful discipline can end well. It can, because the comfort of God arrives in the same breath as the correction.

Looking forward, the passage prepares the church's whole understanding of pastoral life. Every later letter, from Galatians 6:1 to the letters to the seven churches, assumes that rebuke and restoration belong together, and that the aim is life. It also sets up the next movement of the letter. A church whose confidence has been restored and whose heart is soft is ready to be generous, which is where chapters 8 and 9 go.

At the close of the story the sorrow ends for good. The loud voice from the throne says that He will wipe every tear from their eyes, Revelation 21:4. The mourning that was a road to life becomes unnecessary because the life has been reached. What began in Eden as hiding ends in a city where God's people see His face, and where nothing causes regret.

quiz.q: Why did Paul rejoice over the sorrow his letter had caused?

options.text: Because their sorrow led them to genuine repentance, not because they were hurt.
options.note: Paul rejoices in the fruit of repentance, not in their pain itself.

options.text: Because he enjoyed having power to make them grieve.
options.note: Paul explicitly says he does not rejoice that they were made sorrowful.

options.text: Because their sorrow proved they feared him.
options.note: The point is repentance toward God, not fear of Paul.

options.text: Because it settled an old personal grudge.
options.note: Paul acts for their good and God's glory, not personal grievance.

quiz.q: What is the difference between godly sorrow and worldly sorrow?

options.text: Godly sorrow produces repentance leading to salvation; worldly sorrow brings death.
Godly sorrow is more intense; worldly sorrow is milder.
options.note: The difference is direction and fruit, not intensity.

options.text: Godly sorrow is only for pastors; worldly sorrow is for everyone else.
options.note: Both kinds of sorrow are possible for anyone; the issue is where the sorrow leads.

options.text: There is no real difference between them.
options.note: Paul draws a sharp and vital distinction between the two.

quiz.q: What evidence shows the Corinthians' repentance was genuine?

options.text: It produced earnestness, longing, indignation, alarm, zeal, and eagerness to make things right.
options.note: Verse 11 lists the concrete fruits of true repentance.

options.text: They simply felt bad for a while and moved on.
options.note: Feeling bad is not repentance; genuine repentance bears fruit.

options.text: They paid Paul a large sum of money.
options.note: The evidence is changed hearts and action, not payment.

options.text: They wrote an angry reply defending themselves.
options.note: True repentance showed as eagerness to clear themselves before God, not self justification.

quiz.q: How did God comfort the anxious Paul in Macedonia?

options.text: Through the arrival of Titus and his report of the Corinthians' repentance.
options.note: God, who comforts the downcast, comforted Paul by Titus's good news.

options.text: By removing all conflict from his life at once.
options.note: Paul still faced conflicts outside and fears within; comfort came through Titus.

options.text: By a private vision unrelated to the church.
options.note: The comfort came through Titus and the Corinthians' response, not a vision.

options.text: By telling him to abandon the Corinthians.
options.note: God restored the relationship rather than ending it.

questions: Paul distinguishes godly sorrow that leads to life from worldly sorrow that ends in death. When you grieve over sin, does it drive you to God or only into shame and self pity?
True repentance showed itself in concrete fruit, not just feelings. What would earnestness, longing, and zeal to make things right look like in an area you need to repent of?
Paul's painful letter was an act of love, not cruelty. How do you respond to loving correction, and what might God be teaching you through it?
God comforted the downcast Paul through Titus and through the church's response. Who has God used to comfort you, and whom might He want to comfort through you?
Paul's confidence and joy in the Corinthians were fully restored after repentance. Is there a broken relationship where repentance could open the way to renewed trust?

translationNotes.note: Godly sorrow renders lype felt as God intends; the same word covers worldly sorrow, so the difference lies in whether the grief turns the heart to God in repentance, metanoia, or in on itself toward death.
